summary: Describes the NICNAME/WHOIS server and how to access it. With its database, it provides online directory look-up equivalent to the ARPANET Directory. Replaced by RFC 954 and RFC 3912.

plainLanguage.summary: The NICNAME/WHOIS service lets an ARPANET user ask for directory information about a person or handle. It returns text for a person to read, and RFC 812 was later replaced by RFC 954 and RFC 3912.

subtitle: A simple query-and-reply service for looking up ARPANET users

tldr.problem: ARPANET users needed an online directory for finding contact details for other users.
tldr.mechanism: A client connects to SRI-NIC, sends one command line, receives a human-readable answer, and the server closes the connection.
tldr.outcome: RFC 812 was later replaced by RFC 954 and RFC 3912.

today: RFC 812 has been obsoleted by RFC 954 and RFC 3912.

sections.title: The Network Directory
sections.content:
The NICNAME/WHOIS server runs on SRI-NIC and provides directory lookups to ARPANET users. Together with the Identification Data Base, it provides an online lookup equivalent to the ARPANET Directory.

The server returns a user's full name, U.S. mailing address, telephone number and network mailbox. The RFC says the Defense Communications Agency strongly encourages hosts to make the service available to users.
sections.plainLanguage: The service answers requests for a person's name and contact details. Its records are intended to help ARPANET users find one another.

sections.title: Sending a Lookup
sections.content:
A client connects to SRI-NIC using TCP service port 43, or uses the NCP connection procedure described in the RFC. It sends one command line ending with carriage return and line feed, then receives the response. The server closes the connection when it has finished sending output.

The command is normally one name specification. A single question mark asks the server to list the accepted formats. A leading period requests a name-only search, a leading exclamation point requests a handle-only search, and an asterisk before a group argument requests its full membership list.
sections.plainLanguage: Send one search line to the server and wait for its reply. You can add a starting mark to search only names or only handles, and the server closes the connection after answering.

sections.title: Replies for Human Readers
sections.content:
The RFC says replies are not intended to be machine-readable. A client passes the server's text directly to a human user. The examples show a broad search returning several people with the same surname and a more specific search returning a full record.

The document names NICNAME as the global name for the user program, while noting that some sites use the familiar name WHOIS. It recommends NIC-supplied programs because the protocol is expected to evolve.
sections.plainLanguage: The answer is ordinary text for a person to read, not a structured result for another program. A search can return several matching names or a fuller directory entry.
